correctness.rationale: The last letters of the complete greedy arches, followed by a letter absent from the remaining suffix, give a missing subsequence of length one beyond the arch count: each successive earliest match is the corresponding arch endpoint. For counting, the first complete arch has two choices at length two and two at length three. After any arch the terminal run has length one; there are two possible next arches of length two and one of length three, and the optional incomplete suffix has series 1+2t+t^2. With no complete arch the series is 1+2t+2t^2. Summing gives the displayed rational series. Each arch uses two or three bits and the suffix at most two; alternation and (001)^m followed by at most two zeros attain the endpoints, including the empty word case. At u=1 the simple positive dominant pole is separated from the other roots and its numerator is nonzero; analytic continuation gives a uniform exponential remainder locally. Differentiating its inverse-root equation in log u yields the stated first and positive second cumulant slopes, and the centered characteristic functions yield the normal law and rounded threshold. An independent direct count via run compositions and sets of position-subsequences agrees at n=0 through 14.
residual_risks: The replay covers finite histograms, not the analytic limit; the latter is established by the pole argument.
The distribution and limit apply to uniform linear admissible words, not arbitrary regular-language weights or cyclic words.

value.rationale: For a natural regular constraint and a standard measure of scattered-subsequence coverage, the answer gives the exact law at every length, sharp attainable lengths, and a quantitative threshold for randomly sampled constrained words. In particular the small strictly positive variance constant is useful for distinguishing worst-case and typical coverage; it is not given by the generic finite-length algorithm.
residual_risks: This is an explicit tractable model, not an advance for arbitrary alphabets, run caps or sampling laws.
